saves.title: GREMLIN: Museum of Commerce
saves.description:
Nick Herman has spent two decades making sculpture, photography, and books that treat industrial materials and structural systems as raw poetic material — fat solids cast into a lunar-looking frieze, hand-tied nets that sag under their own logic, antennas that double as myth machines. Museum of Commerce, his solo turn at FOYER-LA titled GREMLIN, promises more of that same sleight of hand: taking the leftover vocabulary of manufacturing, retail, and technology and bending it toward something stranger and more bodily.

FOYER-LA is exactly the kind of space this work needs. Founded by artist Connie Walsh in 2019, it operates out of an in-between space — behind a courtyard, in front of a working studio — built for short, dense, experimental projects rather than white-cube spectacle. Herman's MFA is in sculpture from Yale, and his exhibition history runs through Socrates Sculpture Park, LAXART, and the Chinati Foundation's collection, so a project-space outing lets him work at a scale and speed that bigger institutions don't allow.

Given the title's nod to commerce and gremlins alike, expect a show that pokes at consumer culture and the "traumatic residue" — Herman's own phrase — that industry and technology leave on both land and body. It's a compact, single-artist project, which makes it an easy, quick stop for anyone curious about one of LA's more understated sculptor-writers.

saves.title: Unbound
saves.artist: Ariane Callender, Julia Deckman, Mel Deva, Shelly Floyd, Kyle Goderwis, Ashley Perez, Mark Rebennack, Sarah J.
saves.description:
Unbound gathers a roster of K&K's emerging and mid-career artists for a show built entirely around abstraction — work that has, as the gallery puts it, cut loose from realistic representation to chase feeling through layers, color, and line. It's a fitting subject for this Culver City Arts District storefront, which has made a mission of demystifying collecting for first-time buyers rather than chasing museum-scale statements.

Expect a wall of variety rather than a single unifying style: hard-edged geometric compositions next to loose gestural fields, mixed-media surfaces built up in layers, and color-forward pieces that read as much as mood as image. With eight artists sharing the space, the show works like a sampler platter of where non-objective painting is right now among LA's working studio artists — useful for anyone building a collection who wants to see a range of approaches side by side before committing to one.

K&K keeps its shows on a brisk roughly six-week rotation, so Unbound is very much a snapshot rather than a survey — see it while the paint is still fresh on the gallery walls. The opening reception doubled as an informal meet-the-artists mixer, in keeping with the gallery's low-pressure, "art is for everyone" ethos.

saves.title: Vestiges
saves.description:
Alexandra Lopez Iglesias works in paper and clay, two materials she treats less as substances to be shaped than as stand-ins for skin — things that absorb, scar, and record whatever touches them. Vestiges, her solo show at Keystone Art Space, is built from sculptures that use cutting, piercing, tearing, stitching, and scraping to leave visible traces of contact on their surfaces, insisting throughout that these forms aren't metaphors for bodies so much as bodies themselves.

Lopez Iglesias, who was born in Ciudad Juárez and now works in Los Angeles, has built her practice around a fascination with materiality that reportedly goes back to childhood — an early, almost compulsive attention to the textures of the built world around her. That sensitivity to surface and touch carries through into paper especially, a medium she has also taught as a papermaking process in academic settings, giving her sculptures an unusual technical rigor beneath their raw, worked-over look.

The show takes place in Keystone Art Space's daylit gallery inside the artist-studio complex in Lincoln Heights — a fitting context for work that's this tactile and process-driven. It's a short run, just over a week, so this is very much a catch-it-while-you-can show for anyone interested in sculpture that treats the body's history of being touched, held, or neglected as its actual subject matter.

saves.title: Charles Dickson: Select Works, 1966-2026
saves.description:
Charles Dickson has been carving since he was five years old, whittling toy knives under the blankets in South Central Los Angeles, and this survey at Parrasch Heijnen compresses sixty years of that practice into one gallery. Select Works, 1966-2026 pulls from across his career — wood, bronze, concrete, metal, glass, acrylic — tracking a self-taught sculptor who came up alongside Noah Purifoy and John Outterbridge in the Watts arts scene of the late 1960s and never really left it, becoming the longtime artist-in-residence at the Watts Towers Arts Center and groundskeeper of the Towers themselves.

What unites the wildly different materials in Dickson's work is a consistent visual language drawn from African sculptural tradition — masks, totemic forms, ritual tools — repurposed to catalog and honor Black life and history in Los Angeles specifically. He's best known publicly for civic commissions like the Mariposa Metro Green Line station and the Martin Luther King Jr. memorial in Watts, but this gallery presentation gets at the more intimate, studio-based side of his output: carved reliefs, assemblages, and figures that read like a private notebook kept over six decades.

A show spanning 1966 to 2026 is essentially a mini-retrospective, and it's a notable get for a Boyle Heights gallery to present a Los Angeles art-world elder statesman whose work usually turns up in museums and public plazas rather than commercial spaces. Worth seeing both for the sculpture itself and as a rare chance to see this much of Dickson's range in one room.

saves.title: Earth Elements: Paint and Fire
saves.artist: Cosmas and Damian Brown, David Lloyd, Gary Brewer, Cybele Rowe, Roger Herman, Brad Eberhard, Cheyann Washington, Xu DaRocha, Marco Minaya, Galia Linn, Aaron Sheppard
saves.description:
Earth Elements: Paint and Fire, curated by painter Gary Brewer, sets out to catch a group of established painters in the act of switching mediums. Every artist on the checklist has spent years at the easel before turning to clay, and the show is built around what happens to a painter's instincts once color and gesture have to survive a kiln. Expect glazed surfaces that read like brushwork, lumpy forms that behave like still lifes, and a general disregard for the old high-craft rules that used to separate "ceramics" from "art."

The premise leans on real art history — the show's own framing traces a line from George Ohr and Peter Voulkos's studio-pottery rebellion through the Bay Area funk-ceramics arguments of the 1970s that Brewer lived through firsthand, up to painters today who treat clay as just another canvas. Cybele Rowe and Galia Linn, both long associated with large-scale ceramic sculpture, anchor that conversation from the sculpture side, while Roger Herman, Brad Eberhard, Cheyann Washington and the rest arrive as painters testing the material for the first time or the tenth.

It's a gallery known for community-minded, artist-heavy group shows in a converted industrial space in Lincoln Heights, and this one continues that pattern — eleven artists, one curatorial thesis, and a lot of room to see how differently people handle the same physical constraints. Worth a visit for anyone curious about the current cross-traffic between painting and clay in Los Angeles.

saves.title: The Cars of Los Angeles
saves.artist: Carlos Agredano, Merlin Carpenter, Fiona Connor, Sylvie Fleury, Max Göran, Jason Hirata, Alan Michael, Josephine Pryde, Ed Ruscha, Lucien Samaha, Nicole-Antonia Spagnola, Angharad Williams
saves.address: 709 N Hill St #105, Asian Center, Los Angeles, CA 90012
saves.description:
Curated by Dan Mitchell and Richard Sides as a companion to their own two-person show "The Woods" upstairs, this group exhibition treats the automobile as Los Angeles's central cultural artifact and elegy in waiting. The checklist ranges wildly in tone and medium: Carlos Agredano's large canvas built from smog and tire particulate collected off a Lynwood freeway sits near Ed Ruscha photographs and prints of gas stations and studio backlots, while Angharad Williams contributes a sprawling charcoal drawing of a fantasy Maserati and Merlin Carpenter presents a heap of Barbie Ferrari boxes as sculpture. A fabricated "fake John Chamberlain," made from card packaging and spray paint, needles at the market mythology around crushed-car sculpture, and Sylvie Fleury's mixed-media pit-stop installation and vintage beauty-industry video bring her long-running fascination with glamour and speed into the mix.

Video work anchors the show's emotional register: Nicole-Antonia Spagnola's looping silent-film pastiche "Ragged Dick" stages a fatal collision between an early twentieth-century shoeshine boy and a horse-drawn carriage, framing the space to follow as one long meditation on automobility's violence, and Max Göran's "Nothing Runs Like a Deere" extends that unease into contemporary machine culture. Jason Hirata's readymade sculpture built from a catalytic converter and cable spacer, and Fiona Connor's graphite skid mark drawn directly onto the gallery wall, ground the show's more theatrical gestures in blunt, sculptural fact.

It's a smart, dryly funny group show for a city defined by its highways, treating car culture less as subject matter than as a shared American nervous system — one that runs on nostalgia, pollution, and speed in equal measure. The accompanying essay by Sophia Roxane Rohwetter, threading together Gorky's reaction to early cinema and Soviet auto-fiction, gives the show unusual literary heft for what could otherwise read as a novelty theme exhibition.

saves.title: Arreglos Artificiales
saves.address: 3311 E Pico Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90023
saves.description:
Salvador Domínguez opens de boer's fall season with "Arreglos Artificiales" — "artificial arrangements" — a title that plays on the Spanish term for silk-flower bouquets and points toward a practice built on staged, synthetic tableaux. Domínguez, an LA-based painter, works in a hyper-saturated, faintly surreal figurative mode, often placing solitary or paired figures inside interiors thick with pattern, drapery, and decorative objects that feel simultaneously domestic and theatrical.

Based on the works available ahead of the opening, the show looks to continue his interest in the artifice of everyday staging — flowers that don't wilt, rooms arranged for effect rather than comfort — using it as a lens on inherited Latino domestic aesthetics and the performance of hospitality and care. It's a promising follow-up slot after the gallery's summer run of Kash Ford, and a chance to catch an emerging painter's work in a single, focused presentation before the fall art-fair circuit picks up.

saves.title: The Sextant
hours: Wed - Thu Open for school tours only
saves.description:
Enrique Martínez Celaya spent decades as a physicist before turning fully to art, and that background shows in the way he treats memory here less as sentiment than as a structure to be modeled and tested. The Sextant is a scaled-down reconstruction of the modernist house his father built on Cuba's coast between 1957 and 1963 — years that bracketed the Revolution, the Missile Crisis, and the U.S. embargo, and that ended with his family waiting there, never able to leave on their own terms. Rebuilding it as an installation lets Martínez Celaya interrogate what such reconstructions can and cannot recover: the piece is explicit about the gap between the model and the real house, between a childhood remembered and a childhood lived.

Housed at the Wende, a museum built around Cold War-era artifacts and ephemera from behind the Iron Curtain and beyond, the piece fits naturally into the institution's broader project of examining how ordinary lives were shaped by ideological rupture. Rather than photographs or archival objects, though, viewers get an immersive architectural surrogate — a dollhouse-scaled stand-in for a real building that, today, operates as a wedding venue, its political scars mostly invisible to the couples who rent it.

What makes the work worth a visit is its refusal to resolve into either nostalgia or polemic. It sits with the discomfort of authenticity questions — is a reconstruction ever equivalent to the thing itself? — while using a deeply personal family story to gesture at the universal experience of utopian dreams curdling into everyday compromise. It's a quiet, contemplative show, best experienced slowly, and it rewards taking one of the museum's docent-led tours if the schedule allows.

saves.title: Lookout Weekend
saves.description:
The Perez Bros—identical twins Alejandro and Vicente—capture the passion and precision of Los Angeles lowrider culture through painting. This exhibition of new work invites viewers into the garage in the lead-up to a car show or cruise night, featuring scenes of meticulous preparation, tuning, and polishing. The paintings are finished with high-gloss resin and reflective flake, creating a visual surface that mirrors the glossy perfection of the cars themselves and collapses the boundary between subject and medium.

The exhibition title references a 1984 dance track by Debbie Deb that soundtracked the brothers' childhood, setting a tone of hopeful anticipation. While earlier works focus on the cars themselves, this body of work introduces wider scenes, including a panoramic painting of a car show featuring more than a dozen vehicles surrounded by crowds, shade tents, and the bustling community ecosystem that gathers around them. Other works depict cars as near-celebrities, positioned on tow trucks or posed for the camera like stars on a red carpet.

The Perez Bros pull from an extensive photographic archive of the LA lowrider scene, distilling images into scenes of pure detail rendered in bright hues. Their meticulous approach to composition and finish reflects a deep knowledge of and obvious love for the cars and the culture surrounding them—a distinctly Los Angeles subject matter treated with the care of fine art painting.

saves.title: A Certain Slant of Light
saves.artist: Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, Sung Jik Yang
saves.description:
*A Certain Slant of Light* brings together ten artists of different generations and backgrounds to explore how painting, sculpture, and assemblage can interrogate interiority and personal vision. Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, and Sung Jik Yang each navigate their own visual languages—from Coulis's contemplative still lifes and landscapes to Glabush's evocative gestures, from Morse's engagement with environment and narrative to Schmalix's late works reflecting on color and light.

The exhibition emphasizes how these artists, separated by geography and artistic practice, share a commitment to the picture plane as a site of experiential investigation. Their works resist simple categorization: paintings layer abstraction and representation; sculptures occupy the space between material presence and visual illusion. Together, they pose quiet, persistent questions about how we see ourselves and the world around us.

Drawn from different moments in each artist's practice—some historic works, many recent—this group show celebrates the sustained conversations happening within the gallery's roster, where careful observation and emotional resonance remain central to contemporary practice.

sandbox.title: Charles Dickson: Select Works, 1966–2026
sandbox.description: A retrospective spanning six decades of Charles Dickson's practice brings together a selection of works that showcase the artist's evolving vision. Dickson has established himself as a significant figure in contemporary art, working across multiple mediums with a commitment to formal innovation and conceptual rigor. This exhibition presents the breadth of his artistic trajectory, offering viewers an opportunity to trace the continuities and developments that have defined his career from 1966 to the present day. The carefully curated works reveal connections between early investigations and more recent pieces, providing insight into the concerns that have sustained his practice over time.

sandbox.title: Salvador Dominguez: *Arreglos Artificiales*
sandbox.description:
Chicago-based artist Salvador Dominguez presents new work exploring the intersection of domestic culture, identity, and materials. Born in Zacatecas, Mexico, and raised in Greater Los Angeles, Dominguez draws on his lived experience as a first-generation immigrant to create work that engages with language, pattern, and the visual language of everyday life. His practice often references domestic needlepoint patterns and ornamental traditions, translating them into mixed media and encaustic works that occupy a unique space between painting and textile-making. *Arreglos Artificiales* continues this exploration, examining cultural heritage through the lens of decoration and memory. Working between Chicago and Los Angeles, Dominguez's art bridges geographical and cultural divides, asserting the significance of his communities' visual traditions within contemporary art discourse.

This exhibition marks an important moment in the artist's dialogue with de boer's Los Angeles location, deepening the gallery's commitment to artists engaged with questions of cultural identity and immigrant experience.

sandbox.title: Earth Elements: Paint and Fire
sandbox.description:
Curated by Gary Brewer, *Earth Elements: Paint and Fire* brings together painters who have turned to ceramic sculpture and ceramic artists who infuse painterly sensibility into their three-dimensional work. The exhibition draws from the history of ceramic liberation—from George Ohr's early innovations through Peter Voulkos's abstract expressionist ceramics and the irreverent, conceptually sophisticated practice of artists like Viola Frey and Robert Arneson. Rather than remaining bound by craft traditions, the artists in this show approach ceramic material as a tabula rasa, applying a painter's intuition and freedom to the medium.

Two exceptions prove revealing: Galia Linn, who began as a ceramic sculptor and later expanded into painting, and Cybele Rowe, whose monumental ceramic sculptures integrate decades of painterly sensibility into what she terms "volumetric paintings." The exhibition asserts that the boundaries between painting and sculpture, between art and craft, are increasingly fluid and that the most vital contemporary work emerges when artists move fluidly across these traditional divisions.

sandbox.title: Alexandra Lopez Iglesias: *Vestiges*
sandbox.description:
Los Angeles–based artist Alexandra Lopez Iglesias, originally from Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, México, presents a new body of work exploring materiality and the body's encounter with materials. Through paper and clay sculptures, Lopez Iglesias creates and investigates remnants—traces left by touch, care, neglect, and time. Her practice is rooted in a lifelong fascination with texture and material properties, a sensibility evident since childhood. Paper and clay function not as metaphors but as bodies themselves, capable of absorbing, archiving, and resisting in equal measure.

The artist approaches her materials through acts of cutting, piercing, tearing, stitching, scraping, and scarring—gestures that reveal beauty within vulnerability. *Vestiges* invites viewers into intimate encounters where the personal becomes universal, where examining one body illuminates the possibility of transformation in others. The exhibition suggests that the simple act of truly seeing another—materially, emotionally, spiritually—carries profound possibility.

sandbox.title: Ivana Dama: Breathing Alarms
sandbox.description:
New York–based artist Ivana Dama transforms the Wende Museum's East German guardhouse into an immersive sound installation powered entirely by human breath. At the center of *Breathing Alarms* is a custom air-raid siren, a device historically tied to surveillance and protection, that only sounds when visitors breathe into it. The siren's intensity modulates with each person's breath while simultaneously activating an animation of birds circling inside a bespoke aluminum zoetrope—a collision of mechanical watchfulness and organic life.

Dama's research into sirens draws on her own formative experience growing up in post-communist Belgrade during the 1999 NATO bombing, when the sounds and vibrations of air-raid sirens shaped her understanding of how sound carries trauma and memory. *Breathing Alarms* elevates this personal history into a collective experience, inviting visitors to recognize their own breath as a generator of acoustic power. The work reveals how air, sound, and motion underlie the technologies we often take for granted—and how shared physical presence can transform instruments of control into instruments of connection.

Developed in collaboration with MIT's Center for Bits and Atoms, the installation merges cutting-edge digital fabrication with analog mechanics, creating a deeply interactive work about perception, surveillance, and the politics of breath in a moment of environmental and social crisis. It's a rare chance to experience contemporary sound art that's simultaneously intimate, politically engaged, and revelatory about the human body's capacity to generate meaning.

The Perez Bros — identical twins Alejandro and Vicente Perez, who grew up around their father's car club in South Gate — paint lowriders with the fanatical attention of people who have spent a lifetime looking at them. This second solo show with Charlie James Gallery follows the cars out of the spotlight and into the garage, focusing on the tune-ups, polishes, and quiet rituals of preparation that precede a cruise night or car show. It's a shift from spectacle to labor, though the brothers' signature high-gloss resin and reflective flake finishes still make every canvas look like it just rolled off a detailing table.

The paintings on view range from intimate two-figure scenes of men polishing club cars in a driveway to a shaped canvas modeled on a lowrider's spare tire, chrome decal and all. Elsewhere the cars themselves become the subject of near-celebrity treatment — a 1964 Impala chauffeured on a tow truck, too precious for LA's potholed streets, or a car posed like it's fielding paparazzi. The show builds toward its largest work yet, a panoramic scene of a car show crowded with parked cars, shade tents, and clustered onlookers, widening the brothers' usual close-up frame to take in the community that lowrider culture actually runs on.

Both Perez brothers trained in painting at Otis College of Art and Design before turning their shared archive of car-club photography into a collaborative practice, and their work has become a fixture of LA's Chicano art scene precisely because it treats lowriding as culture worth this kind of formal seriousness — mirrors, chrome inlay, and mural-bright color used not as gimmick but as a way of matching a painting's surface to its subject's own obsessive shine. For anyone who knows the difference between a cruise night and a car show, or wants to, this is a rare gallery treatment of a subculture usually seen only in parking lots.

real.title: Lookout Weekend
real.description:
The Perez Bros—identical twins Alejandro and Vicente—capture the passion and precision of Los Angeles lowrider culture through painting. This exhibition of new work invites viewers into the garage in the lead-up to a car show or cruise night, featuring scenes of meticulous preparation, tuning, and polishing. The paintings are finished with high-gloss resin and reflective flake, creating a visual surface that mirrors the glossy perfection of the cars themselves and collapses the boundary between subject and medium.

The exhibition title references a 1984 dance track by Debbie Deb that soundtracked the brothers' childhood, setting a tone of hopeful anticipation. While earlier works focus on the cars themselves, this body of work introduces wider scenes, including a panoramic painting of a car show featuring more than a dozen vehicles surrounded by crowds, shade tents, and the bustling community ecosystem that gathers around them. Other works depict cars as near-celebrities, positioned on tow trucks or posed for the camera like stars on a red carpet.

The Perez Bros pull from an extensive photographic archive of the LA lowrider scene, distilling images into scenes of pure detail rendered in bright hues. Their meticulous approach to composition and finish reflects a deep knowledge of and obvious love for the cars and the culture surrounding them—a distinctly Los Angeles subject matter treated with the care of fine art painting.

sandbox.title: A Certain Slant of Light
sandbox.artist: Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, Sung Jik Yang
sandbox.description:
Philip Martin Gallery has assembled ten painters and sculptors of very different generations and temperaments for a show built around the idea of interior light — literal and psychological. The lineup spans a late Los Angeles conceptualist (Carl Cheng), a group of mid-career West Coast painters known for pattern, color, and landscape (Holly Coulis, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Sky Glabush), and younger or more recently arrived voices working in miniature realism and collage-inflected fantasy (Sophie Treppendahl, Aaron Morse, Sung Jik Yang), alongside the late Austrian-born painter Hubert Schmalix. It's a deliberately loose curatorial premise, closer to a mood board than a thesis, that lets each artist's handling of light and interiority stand on its own.

Aaron Morse's contribution, a large canvas of the volcanic Red Hill cinder cone in the Coso Range, extends his ongoing interest in frontier mythology and 19th-century Romantic landscape painting, while Sophie Treppendahl's jewel-sized, candlelit domestic interiors continue the hushed, still-life intimacy that has become her signature. Pamela Jorden's webbed abstractions and Christy Matson's textile-based work (shown alongside the paintings) bring a tactile, handmade counterpoint to the more illusionistic pieces by Korty and Schmalix.

Taken together, the show reads as a survey of how painters right now are thinking about atmosphere and glow — sunlight through a window, a candle on a table, the volcanic light of a desert landscape — without forcing those disparate approaches into false unity. It's a good entry point into the gallery's roster and a chance to see a late Schmalix painting alongside artists two generations his junior.

real.title: A Certain Slant of Light
real.artist: Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, Sung Jik Yang
real.description:
*A Certain Slant of Light* brings together ten artists of different generations and backgrounds to explore how painting, sculpture, and assemblage can interrogate interiority and personal vision. Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, and Sung Jik Yang each navigate their own visual languages—from Coulis's contemplative still lifes and landscapes to Glabush's evocative gestures, from Morse's engagement with environment and narrative to Schmalix's late works reflecting on color and light.

The exhibition emphasizes how these artists, separated by geography and artistic practice, share a commitment to the picture plane as a site of experiential investigation. Their works resist simple categorization: paintings layer abstraction and representation; sculptures occupy the space between material presence and visual illusion. Together, they pose quiet, persistent questions about how we see ourselves and the world around us.

Drawn from different moments in each artist's practice—some historic works, many recent—this group show celebrates the sustained conversations happening within the gallery's roster, where careful observation and emotional resonance remain central to contemporary practice.
